forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Rochdale's pension asset improved by £18.3m but accounting rules prevent it showing in accounts
news_drafts.lead: Rochdale's latest actuarial valuation of its pension fund shows a net asset that has improved by £18.3 million, the Audit and Governance Committee heard on 24 September. However, accounting standards (IFRIC 14) impose an asset ceiling that limits the recognised net pension asset on the council's balance sheet to nil. The improvement therefore does not flow through to the financial statements. The auditors also identified and the council corrected a misstatement in which £14.75 million of Public Works Loan Board loans had been classified as short-term borrowing rather than long-term, which changes the council's debt maturity profile and refinancing schedule. The auditors said they were awaiting final responses on valuations of land and buildings, investment properties including the Manchester Airport shareholding, and pension fund assurance, but anticipate issuing an unqualified audit opinion once these matters are resolved.

findings.headline: Pension asset improved by £18.346m in actuarial valuation but accounting ceiling limits recognised balance sheet asset to nil
findings.detail: The final IAS 19 actuarial report increased the net pension asset by £18.346m from the draft position. However, the asset ceiling required under IFRIC 14 accounting standards limits the council's recognised net pension asset in the balance sheet to nil. The improvement therefore does not flow through to the financial statements.
findings.matters: While the balance sheet position is unchanged, a £18.3m improvement in the underlying actuarial pension position indicates the council's long-term liability position is improving—important context for assessing the council's true financial sustainability and workforce affordability.
findings.quote: The updated actuarial valuation resulted in an increase of £18.346m in the Net Pension Asset. However, due to the application of the asset ceiling, which limits the Council's recognised Net Pension Asset to nil, there was no impact on the amounts recognised in the Balance Sheet.

findings.headline: £14.75 million PWLB loan reclassified from short-term to long-term borrowing, correcting classification error
findings.detail: The auditors identified and the council corrected a misstatement where PWLB loans were originally classified as short-term (due within one year) rather than long-term borrowing. This changes the council's debt maturity profile and refinancing schedule.
findings.matters: Debt maturity profile determines when the council must refinance, affecting refinancing risk and cash flow planning—core concerns for both lenders deciding on new borrowing and finance directors managing liquidity.
findings.quote: PWLB loans have been reclassified from short-term to long-term borrowing to correct an error in the original classification.

findings.headline: Audit work still in progress across multiple material asset valuations as of committee meeting date
findings.detail: The auditors note they are awaiting responses on land and buildings valuation testing, investment property valuations including Manchester Airport shareholding, and pension fund auditor assurance, among other items. An unqualified opinion is anticipated but remains conditional on satisfactory resolution of these outstanding matters.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs a completed audit to have confidence in the council's reported financial position. Outstanding matters on major asset classes represent open questions about the true value of the balance sheet.
findings.figures: Multiple areas noted: Land and Buildings (£432m total assets), Investment Properties including Manchester Airport, Pension Fund assets
findings.quote: Our audit procedures for the year ended 31 March 2026 are still in progress as at the date of issuing this report.

findings.headline: Health & Social Care Pool Budget overspend of £6.4m; Local Authority contribution increased to £182.5m against £175.7m budget
findings.detail: The pooled budget with the health service shows total expenditure of £215.3m against a forecast of £208.9m. The council's own contribution rose to £182.5m from a budgeted £175.7m — a £6.8m increase. This reflects overspends in both Children's and Adults pooled services.
findings.matters: Pooled budgets can mask the council's exposure; this shows the council is bearing the cost of health service demand it cannot control. The council absorbs its share of overspends under the Section 75 agreement.
findings.figures: Pool budget overspend £6.4m; Council contribution £182.5m vs £175.7m budget (£6.8m overage)
findings.quote: Pool budget expenditure is higher than budgeted, primarily due to overspends against local authority Children's and Adults Social Care budgets addressed elsewhere in this report. Under the existing Section 75 agreement both partners are responsible for their own variation to budget and so both partners contributions have been amended to reflect the variation to budget.

findings.headline: Equalisation Reserve drawn down by £1.322m to fund in-year overspend; this is the residual after all other services' savings
findings.detail: The overall council position would have been a £4.725m overspend before reserves. Other directorates achieved £5.5m in in-year savings, leaving a net £1.322m overspend that was funded from the Equalisation Reserve. This is a one-off fix and signals that the council's baseline budget does not cover its costs.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns are not sustainable. A lender needs to know the reserve balance and trajectory; if this is a recurring pattern, reserves will be depleted and there is no buffer for unforeseen pressure.
findings.figures: £1.322m drawn from Equalisation Reserve; £5.5m in directorate savings offset £6.824m Children's Services overspend
findings.quote: The 2025/26 Revenue outturn position is a £1.322m overspend which is to be funded from the Equalisation reserve, as agreed at Budget Fixing Council in February 2026. The overspend has primarily arisen from pressures in Children's Services with an overspend position of £6.8m. This has been partially offset by savings in the other services totalling £5.5m.
